nutshell: Occluded visible-infrared person ReID is doubly hard: occlusions and the visible/infrared modality gap both disrupt spatial feature alignment, and occlusions often land in different places in each modality's image. SFCL adds a frequency-domain branch alongside the usual spatial features - decomposing deep features into FFT amplitude (modality-specific style) and phase (modality-consistent structure), aligning amplitude/phase across modalities via an optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) module, then injecting these frequency priors back into the spatial features - on the reasoning that phase information stays more stable than raw spatial appearance under both occlusion and modality shift. The paper also introduces two new occluded cross-modality benchmarks built from realistic, semantically placed synthetic occlusions rather than random block masking.
contributions: Cross-Modality Frequency Alignment Module (CFAM): FFT-decomposes visible/infrared deep features into amplitude and phase, refines each with a Trans-Mamba block (Vmamba for the amplitude branch, Transformer for the phase branch), then aligns cross-modality amplitude and phase distributions via a Cross-modality Frequency Sinkhorn (CFS) module that solves an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem to redistribute infrared spectral energy toward the visible domain.

Spatial-Frequency Interaction Module (SFIM): injects the CFAM's frequency-domain output back into spatial features via a learned spatial-frequency correlation map, Gabor-based suppression of occlusion-induced high-frequency noise, and cross-covariance pooling between the two domains to produce a compact, occlusion-robust fused representation.

Frequency-Aware Discriminative (FAD) loss: combines a cross-modality frequency contrastive term (aligning VIS/NIR spectral embeddings) with a semantic-consistency term (KL divergence between each modality's predicted class distribution and its cross-modal K-nearest-neighbor-averaged distribution) to jointly regularize the frequency and semantic spaces.

Two new occluded VI-ReID benchmarks, Occ-SYSU-MM01 and Occ-RegDB, built with a YOLOv8-seg + SAM 'Semantic Occlusion Library' of real object instances placed using scene/position/size priors and adapted to NIR appearance via grayscale normalization, histogram alignment, and Gaussian smoothing - designed to be more realistic than the random-rectangle/block-masking occlusion protocols used by prior occluded ReID work.
deficiencies: The text claims a '+6.57% Rank-1 gain over the baseline' on Occ-SYSU-MM01, but Table 1 itself shows baseline R1=59.22 vs. full-model R1=65.97 - a 6.75-point gap, not 6.57. The companion '+4.88%' claim for the Occ-RegDB ablation has no corresponding ablation table anywhere in the paper (Table 1 only covers Occ-SYSU-MM01), so it can't be checked at all.

The introduction states the 'only' prior cross-modality approach to occluded VI-ReID is reference [5] ('Occluded visible-infrared person re-identification,' TMM 2023) - which shares three authors (Yujian Feng, Yimu Ji, Fei Wu, including this paper's corresponding author) with this submission. That overlap isn't disclosed, and [5] (as 'OCMF') is also used as a direct competitor baseline in Tables 2-3, worth knowing when weighing how independent the 'comparison with the field' really is for this specific sub-task.

The full model (CFAM+SFIM+FAD) roughly triples parameter count (23.55M to 70.50M) and more than doubles FLOPs (9.21G to 22.26G) and inference latency (0.40ms to 1.25ms) versus the baseline, which the paper characterizes as the accuracy gain coming 'with a moderate increase in inference cost' - no accuracy-per-parameter or accuracy-per-FLOP comparison against a compute-matched baseline is offered to support that characterization.

Every one of the 12 baseline methods' numbers in the headline Occ-SYSU-MM01/Occ-RegDB comparison (Table 2) had to be reproduced by this paper's own team, since these two occluded benchmarks are introduced by this same paper - none of those methods have official published numbers on this exact benchmark to cross-check against, so the reproduction's fairness (tuning effort per baseline) can't be independently verified from the paper alone.
notable: The FAD loss (Table 1, Index 3 to Index 4) is free at inference time - parameter count, FLOPs, and latency are identical between the SFIM-only and SFIM+FAD rows (70.50M / 22.26G / 1.25ms) - yet it produces the largest single Rank-1 jump in the whole ablation (+2.18, from 63.79 to 65.97), making it arguably the most cost-effective individual component, though the paper doesn't explicitly call this out. Also notable: the occlusion-construction pipeline itself (YOLOv8-seg + SAM 'Semantic Occlusion Library,' scene/position/size-aware placement, cross-modality NIR-style adaptation) is a reusable recipe for building realistic synthetic occlusion benchmarks in any ReID or detection setting currently relying on random block-masking as a weak occlusion proxy.
